title: The preliminaries
hookLine: first point: the four thoughts that turn the mind

lines: SKIP IT AND THE DISH FALLS APART.
cards: Onions first. Before anything goes in the pan, the cook peels, chops, measures, sets out the salt. Nobody posts a photo of that part.
It's slow, it smells, and it isn't the dish. But skip it, and the dish falls apart halfway through, with something burning while you hunt for the garlic. Mind training opens the same way.
Before the well-known practices, before the slogans about dreams and patience, the very first line of the text says, in effect, start with the groundwork.

teach.b: First, the slogan. The opening line of the seven points is usually given as: first, train in the preliminaries. The whole rest of the text stands on them.

teach.h: FOUR THOUGHTS THAT TURN THE MIND.
teach.b: Tibetan commentaries explain them as four thoughts that turn the mind. One: this human life is precious and hard to come by. Two: it will end, and nobody knows when.
Three: actions have results, and they follow you. Four: the round of samsara, however you rearrange it, doesn't satisfy. Third, if that sounds familiar, it should.
Last week the lamrim walked through these same four, a day each.
Here they come back, packed tight, as the ground floor of mind training, and that repetition is the point.
Tibetan teachers say a student doesn't graduate from the preliminaries; the basics get revisited at the start of a session, a day, a hard week. Fourth, why they turn the mind.
Picture a cart rolling one way out of habit: toward comfort, distraction, more of the same.

teach.h: A HAND ON THE CART, TURNING IT.
teach.b: The four thoughts are a hand on the shaft, turning it, not by force, but by seeing clearly.
If life is precious, short, consequential and not fixable by rearranging, then, in this teaching, training the heart stops looking like a hobby.
Only after that turn does Chekawa's text go on to the main practice, and tomorrow, so do these lessons.

how: Tibetan Buddhist practitioners often begin a session by bringing to mind the four thoughts that turn the mind: precious human life, death and impermanence, karma, and the faults of samsara.

games.q: you're eager to get to the well-known practices of mind training. the text's first line is about something else. what does it ask?
o: skip ahead to the main practice.
games.why: the opening line is usually given as: first, train in the preliminaries. the main practice comes after the turn.

practice: Give each of the four thoughts a few slow breaths: this life, precious, rare, here right now; this life, ending, time unknown; what I do, bearing results; the round, unsatisfying however I rearrange it.
Don't argue with them or polish them; let each land, like ingredients set out on the counter, and notice whether anything in you turns, even slightly.

wordCard.voice: The preliminaries. The first of the seven points: four thoughts that turn the mind, the groundwork for everything after. Today's word.
